questions.title: What is the standard for granting a stay pending appeal and how did the Ninth Circuit apply it in Pacito v. Trump?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites the four‑factor test from *Nken v. Holder* and says the first two factors are “most critical.” I’m confused about how the court weighed each factor here, especially the likelihood of success on the merits for the government’s claim that the President’s authority under 8 U.S.C. § 1182(f) is unreviewable. Did the court consider the plaintiffs’ arguments under the APA at all when deciding the stay?

questions.title: Does 8 U.S.C. § 1182(f) give the President unreviewable discretion to suspend refugee admissions, or is the action subject to any judicial review?
questions.question_body: The majority says the President “has undoubtedly fulfilled” the statutory finding requirement and that the court should not conduct a “searching inquiry” into his justification. Is that a declaration that the provision is non‑justiciable, or does the court still retain authority to review whether the finding was arbitrary or contrary to law?

questions.title: Is 8 U.S.C. § 1522 a mandatory funding command or merely an authorization for refugee resettlement services?
questions.question_body: Judge Lee argues that the word “authorization” in the title makes the provision permissive, while the majority treats the statutory “shall” language in § 1522(a) as creating a mandatory duty. How do courts typically interpret the interplay between the permissive language in the title and the mandatory language in the body of a statute?

questions.title: How does the APA apply to the State Department’s termination of cooperative agreements for refugee resettlement?
questions.question_body: The Ninth Circuit notes that the government is “not likely to prevail on at least one of plaintiffs’ challenges under the APA.” What specific APA provisions (e.g., notice-and-comment, arbitrary and capricious standard) are implicated when the executive abruptly ends funding contracts, and how might the plaintiffs prove a violation?

questions.title: What is the legal effect of a district court’s preliminary injunction when the appellate court stays it “in its entirety except as noted,” and how does that affect the parties’ obligations on the ground?
questions.question_body: After the appellate stay, the district court orders are stayed, but the order also mentions a limited carve‑out for conditionally approved refugees. How should the parties interpret which actions are permissible during the stay, especially regarding ongoing terminations of cooperative agreements?

questions.title: Can the President’s suspension of refugee admissions under § 1182(f) be challenged on due‑process or equal‑protection grounds, or are those claims pre‑empted by the immigration discretion doctrine?
questions.question_body: The opinion focuses on statutory authority, but the plaintiffs might argue constitutional violations. Is there any precedent that allows constitutional claims to survive a claim of broad presidential discretion in immigration matters?

questions.title: What is the significance of the “limited carve‑out” for individuals conditionally approved for refugee status before Jan. 20, 2025, in the stay order?
questions.question_body: The panel stayed the preliminary injunction “to the extent the district court’s order applies to individuals who were conditionally approved….” I’m unclear on why the court treated that group differently and what legal reasoning supports carving out that subset while staying the rest.

questions.title: How does the “broad discretion” doctrine from *Trump v. Hawaii* interact with the statutory requirements of the Refugee Act of 1980 in this case?
questions.question_body: The majority leans heavily on deference to the President, yet the Refugee Act sets out a comprehensive framework for admission and assistance. Does the Refugee Act limit the President’s discretion under § 1182(f), or can the President override the Act’s provisions by simply finding a detriment to U.S. interests?
